utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am. Out of the accused, only the accused Beara is not present today. I take it, Mr. Ostojic, that we will be receiving his waiver in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. You will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Prosecution, I think the position is exactly the same as yesterday as regards your presentation, so let's start. Mr. Haynes, good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, yesterday afternoon when we finished off, we were discussing or we had just begun to discuss the brigade rules of the JNA of 1984. Before we get into a further discussion, as it were, as to their legality, purpose, and application, I'd just like to cover a few, rather, more basic facts about them. Before you became commander of the Zvornik Brigade in December of 1992, had you ever had the opportunity to study the brigade rules of the JNA of 1984?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had such an opportunity, and I did start studying these rules, but I didn't study all the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I don't want to lead you. During which period of your military career and education was that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was during the 20-day period when I was in the Staff school, Command Staff School. I was previously aware of the fact that such rules did exist, but I didn't have a copy of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Which leads me to my next question. When you arrived at the Zvornik Brigade in December of 1992 and the Command at Orahovac, was there a copy of the brigade rules there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. The Command was based in Orahovac. As for the library that used to be in the Territorial Defence Staff before, I don't know whether there was such a library -- whether there was such a copy there. I saw some of the rules, but I can't really tell you which rules I saw, or I saw certain sets of rules, and there were probably the brigade rules among them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just to complete the point: Other than you, was there anybody else in the Command or Staff who at that time had any familiarity with them at all?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Chief of Staff was familiar with those rules. As far as I can remember, it's on the basis of those rules that he compiled sort of a summary on the obligations of certain organs of the Staff and of the Staff, summary on the duties they should perform. But I can't be certain whether he had a copy of those rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I just want to recap, as it were, towards the end of yesterday's session. We just dealt briefly with the legal force of those rules, and we looked at the instruction at the head of them. What was your understanding of the legal force of the brigade rules in 1984?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, given that I was previously a lot more familiar with the battalion rules, because those are the rules that I used, and given that they are quite similar to this other set of rules, I had a general position and approach with regard to rules of that kind, and I can say that those rules - and that's the case for other rules too - were issued on the basis of instructions or directives on professional military textbooks or literature. So that's the kind of literature we're dealing with. It wasn't issued on the basis of law, and adhering to the provisions of those rules or not adhering to them didn't result in any legal action. These rules also had certain ideological elements that were the result of the idea of general People's Defence, and this is based on the socialist self-management system. These were rules that governed doctrine or related to doctrine, which would change over time, and these rules related to an army that no longer existed at the time. However, these rules did provide instructions and aided one in training officers and command staff in order to make it possible for them to perform their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can we move straight to the heart of the matter, please, and have a look at Article 115. So can we have in e-court, please, for the benefit of Mr. Pandurevic P694, page 64 in the B/C/S and page 37 in the English. Something very interesting has appeared in e-court in the English channel.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document seems to be only in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We're looking for P694. I just better check that. That wasn't a document that should have been kept secret or anything? Okay. I'll repeat that. It's page 64 in the B/C/S. You have 37 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We can all see it, but: "The brigade commander has the exclusive right to command all brigade units and attached units. He bears full responsibility for the work of the brigade command and subordinate commands, for the state of morale, for security and combat readiness, for training, and for the proper performance of tasks. The commander takes decisions, assigns tasks to units, monitors their fulfillment, and demands their strict execution regardless of difficulties that arise. Through his personal conduct, work and involvement in the implementation of policies, ethical standing, courage, ability, fairness, cool-headedness, consistency, and respect for personality and opinions of subordinates, the commander vitally influences the entire condition of the brigade, especially the morale of the units in command." Do you agree with that as a basic statement of principle?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How does that paragraph help us to determine what happens if, for example, the brigade commander is absent for any reason?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first, I should say that you'll find such items in all the rules that concern battalions, brigades, divisions, corps; and this item is based on the idea of command and control and primarily on the principle of singleness of control. This principle, this idea, means that only one man can be in command of one unit, of a given unit. This can be the commander of a brigade, for example, in this case, who was designated to be the commander. Someone who represents the brigade commander at any given point in time can also act under this item, or an individual appointed or designated by the superior command. So this idea of singleness of command is included in this item. The second item -- or, rather, the second paragraph means that the commander has to be a member of the League of Communists. If we apply this to the VRS, then he would have to be a member of the leading party or, rather, the party in power. That wasn't the case in the VRS. This rule -- rather, this item doesn't take into consideration certain possibilities that are set forth in certain other rules, and that has to do with the absence of the commander or the fact that he is prevented from performing his duties. If this item was applied in literal terms, one could say that the brigade is dead and no one could command the brigade, and that can never be the case. The unit must never remain without a commander or an officer. This is a basic military rule. So this item is applicable to each and every officer who, at a given point in time, has command over a given unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. In the English, the whole of the next article, Article 116, is on the screen. I think it is in the B/C/S, as well, but let's go to that, please, Article 116: "The Staff is the main organ of the brigade command, and it functionally links and integrates the operations of all the command organs. "The Chief of Staff directs the work of the Staff. He is also the deputy commander of the brigade. The Chief of Staff, in accordance with the commander's decisions, has the right to assign tasks to subordinates. "The Staff consists of an operations and training organ, an intelligence organ, a recruitment and personnel organ, organs for combat arms, and the office." Firstly, the statement there that the Chief of Staff, in accordance with the commander's decisions, has the right to assign tasks to subordinates. What, practically, does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Chief of Staff is in a brigade if the establishment provides for this. There are certain brigades where there is no Chief of Staff. In this case, we're talking about Chief of Staff. In Article 116, when it says that the Chief of Staff, in accordance with the commander's decision, has the right to assign tasks to subordinates, well, in this case "assigns tasks to subordinates" is put in a very subtle manner. This means that he doesn't have the original right to command brigade units. What does this mean? It means that there has to be at least one condition, and that is that the brigade commander is on site and in command of the brigade, and he took a decision, and then the Chief of Staff, in accordance with that decision, assigns tasks to units, and he is then de facto playing the role of Chief of Staff and not the role of deputy commander. Here, it isn't said that the deputy commander issues tasks as a commander. It says the Chief of Staff, so his role is a twofold one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I'd like to move on from there because we're going to come to deal explicitly with the question of the absence of the commander. Was the situation where the brigade commander was absent from the brigade regulated by military law within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was regulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't want to give you a memory test, but do you recall the name of the rules or regulations that regulated it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For every command level, from the level of brigades, regiments, corps, and at higher levels, for each level there are special documents that regulate the responsibilities of the commander, and these are the rules on the responsibility of the command for regiments, brigades, divisions, corps, and so on and so forth. So this is a document that is legally binding, and it means that the commander has to abide by the provisions of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have, please, into e-court 7D717, and we'll begin by looking at the first page of the document to underline the point that Mr. Pandurevic has just made, and I'm grateful for it being pointed out to me that there has been additional translation of this document, so I have to ask for the complete version to be put into e-court, please. Thank you. Just page 2 in the English; 3, maybe. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: These are the rules on responsibility of the command in a brigade or regiment, and at the top there we see the, as it were, legal authority of these rules, and in English it reads: "Pursuant to Article 7, item 8, on the Law of the Yugoslav People's Army and the authorisation by the Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces of the SFRY, I hereby issue rules on responsibility of the commander of brigade and regiment." You've probably already answered this, but what does that tell us about the rules that we're looking at now?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This means that the rules are based on the laws or, rather, the Law on the Yugoslav People's Army, and on the title page you can say that this is a confidential document and it has a registration number.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just to repeat an exercise we carried out with the brigade rules, were these rules on which you'd received any training or education prior to becoming a brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, no. I was familiar with certain general matters, but I wasn't familiar with these rules then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, again, do you know whether a set of these rules was present at the brigade command of the Zvornik Brigade during 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly didn't have a copy. As to whether there was such a copy somewhere, I couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now can we have a look at page 5, probably in both of the documents. We're looking for Article 10. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "The commander is responsible for the overall situation of the brigade or regiment, for the correct and lawful work of the command organs, and for the successful and timely completion of all tasks within the remit of the command organs. "The commander has direct control over the brigade and regiment units through the Chief of Staff, his assistants, and the organs for combat arms." Does that accord with your understanding of the brigade commander's legal responsibility?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. It does agree with my understanding of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we now move forward one page to page 6 in both documents and have a look at Article 17.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: "In the absence of the commander, the Chief of Staff or deputy commander stand in for him with all the commander's rights and duties." Is that your understanding of what the legal responsibility was of the Chief of Staff or deputy commander in the absence of the commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And perhaps you could explain to us how this provision interacts, as it were, with the articles of the brigade rules we were just looking at, Articles 115 and 116.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Articles 115 and 116 from the brigade rules and Articles 10 and 17 on the powers of the commands of the regiment are somewhat different. In Article 115, a principle has been applied without any elaboration, and the power on the commander has been absolutised [as interpreted]. As a human being and in professional terms, in these articles what happens, the commander is defined as the one who commands the units of the brigade immediately and through the Staff and his assistants. If we were to apply Article 115 from the brigade rules, we could understand that the commander needs only a typist and a courier, nobody else in the Command. However, this book of rules elaborates that somewhat further in a more precise way. In Article 116 of the brigade rules, the only thing that is said is that the Chief of Staff is also the commander's deputy. However, Article 17 explains that, and it says that in his absence, the commander may be replaced by the Chief of Staff or the deputy commander with all the rights and responsibilities of the commander, which means that that person acts on behalf of the commander and has to act pursuant to Article 115 of the brigade rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, earlier on you did say that the legal rights and duties of the commander and the Chief of Staff were regulated at every level, and just to illustrate that point I wonder if you could have a quick look, please, at P410. We want to see Article 10. It's page 8 in the English and page 10 in the B/C/S, and this is to show the position at corps level. This is P410, the regulations on the responsibilities of the land army corps command in peacetime, and it reads: "Article 10. The Chief of Staff shall replace the commander when the latter is absent and shall have all rights and duties. If the commander and Chief of Staff are both absent at the same time, the commander shall be replaced by the officer assigned on the order of the commander." Was that the provision you had in mind when you told us earlier that these matters were regulated by law at every level of the army?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can see that the provisions of this article as well as of the previous articles are the same. If we were to look at a division book of rules, we would find a similar provision, i.e., if we were to look at the book of rules on the division commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I apologise to the court manager for this, but can we now go back to 7D717 and have a look at the second part of Article 17 to see the position in relation to the brigade and regiment if both the commander and the Chief of Staff are absent. I think in the B/C/S, we'll need to go over one more page. Yes, I knew this was coming. It reads in the English: "If the commander and the Chief of Staff are absent, one of the assistant commanders shall be ordered to stand in."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you glean that from the, as it were, bad scanning of the document in B/C/S, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And does that describe the situation in law as you understood it to be if both you and your Chief of Staff were absent from the brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This describes a situation when both a commander and a Chief of Staff are absent; it will be the corps commander who will regulate that matter and order which officer will perform the duties of the commander in such a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. You anticipated the next question. I suppose it's not beyond the bounds of possibility that a set of circumstances would arise where the commander and the Chief of Staff were both absent and there was no time or no possibility for the corps commander to order one of the assistants to stand in. What would happen then?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very clear that life cannot be regulated in all of its segments by rules and regulations and instructions. Situations arise in life when one has to react promptly and spontaneously. If both the commander and the Chief of Staff or his deputy are all absent for whatever reason, at that moment the Command should be taken over by the most senior officer who is in the Command, or, rather, the corps commander should appoint somebody from the corps command, an officer, that is, who would be in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And I just want to come to a couple more provisions to deal with that point. Can we have a look, please, at P26, and we can move through this document very briefly, Mr. Pandurevic, a document headed "The organisational and establishment structure of the army Corps, the Main Staff of the Army of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina," dated the 26th of May, 1992. In brief, what did you understand this document to be?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We know that the Army of Republika Srpska was officially established pursuant to a decision of the Assembly of Republika Srpska on the 12th of May, 1992, and we can see that this order was drafted on the 26th of May, 1992, and it was created as a result of the process of negotiations and counselling between the highest political and military leaderships in the Republika Srpska, and the topic was how to organise the Army of Republika Srpska. It doesn't say anywhere here that one should start from the existing doctrine that had been in use by the Yugoslav People's Army or that the establishment books should be used that had already existed. It says here that one has to start from the specific circumstances and that brigades should be established in keeping with the abilities and conditions under which parts of the Territorial Defence existed. This is a creative approach to the organisation of the military which was applied by the Main Staff and the Supreme Commander. In one place here, it says that the army should be enabled for offensives and to protect Serbian territories in Bosnia and Herzegovina rather than to be able and capable of taking territories that belong to others. This is about a new state being created and a new military being created in that new state.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And now, can we have a look at P147, and we need page 10 in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I've not shown you the first page of this document, but these are the provisional service regulations for the Army of Republika Srpska, dated the 25th of August, 1992. Just remind us: What was your position within that army on the 25th of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: For the record, the document is P417.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I'm speaking too fast, I think, when I give numbers. I will slow down. I promise you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So where were you on the 25th of August, 1992, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, I was in Visegrad. I was the commander of the Light Infantry Brigade of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were a copy of these rules delivered to you at that stage?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. These were temporary regulations that I did not see during the war, but I was familiar with the rules of service of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia, which were very similar to these rules. So in practical terms, the new rules did not present anything new to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And do you know whether a copy of these rules were kept -- or these provisional rules were kept at the Command of the Zvornik Brigade during the time of your command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Can we start by having a look at Article 17: "Members of the army shall carry out the orders of their superiors without demure in full, accurately and punctually. If by chance the order was not given in good time, the person is required to take measures and act in accordance with the specific situation. "Members of the army shall carry out the orders of the most senior officer present when the superior officer is absent." I'll complete it: "The execution of each order shall first be reported to the superior officer or to the officer who has given the order." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Allow me to say, first of all, something in general terms about the relationships in the army. This will make Article 17 clearer. The main relationship in the army is the relationship of command, and this command relationship is based on issuing orders and execution of the orders issued. Here, the subtitle reads "Giving orders." Giving orders is one of the fine functions of command and control. Every officer in the army who has his subordinates, either organs or individuals or units, even, is entitled and is duty-bound to give orders, i.e., to command. Every officer thus, with regard to their subordinates and their superiors, is placed in the command relationship, and this Article 17 regulates precisely these issues. If it had been applied in practice fully, if it was fully applied, it would be much easier to carry out command over the army, if the orders were carried out without demure in full, accurately and punctually. This is what this strives for. In any case, you can see that there is no situation in which an officer would not be found to give orders, and if the situation is such, then any such given order has to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What about the obligations of a soldier under the VRS to carry out the orders of the most senior officer present?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to these rules, he's duty-bound to execute the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does a commanding officer always have to be a commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I tried to explain already. It is not a common expression to say "a commanding officer." A commanding officer does not have to be a commander. There's also the chief of an administration, the chief of department. They also have their subordinates to whom they issue orders, i.e., command them. Also, an officer who is not a commander by function can be assigned temporarily to a task and perform the duties of a commander. This is what my Chief of Staff did. The corps command issued an order to go outside of the zone of responsibility of the corps and carry out the duties of a commander there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What would be the situation were an officer, for example, of the rank of colonel to have given orders to soldiers in one of your units, say, a battalion?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In keeping with these rules, soldiers should act upon such an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now can we have a look at Article 16, "Joint Tasks." "When several units are given a joint task, a commanding officer shall be appointed in good time to direct the execution of the task. If this is not regulated beforehand, the role of superior officer shall be assumed by the most senior officer, who shall direct the execution of the task. If a unit or an institution is suddenly left without a commanding officer, command shall be assumed by his deputy or the highest-ranking officer in that unit until a new officer is appointed." I'm not too worried about the second paragraph. I think we've covered that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you help us as to what your understanding of a joint task is?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A joint task, in itself, implies that several units have to be involved in the execution of that task. This means that there are several participants in the execution of a task. You can have a company from one brigade, a battalion from another brigade, a group from another corps, and they can all appear in the same territory, executing the same task. If it is not regulated, who will be in charge of all these units, who will be in command of all the individuals in the territory, then in keeping with Article 16, para 1, the role of the commander is assumed by the most senior officer among these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What is the smallest army unit in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The smallest organisational unit in the JNA was a department.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: How many soldiers did that comprise?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Detachment. That detachment comprised eight to ten soldiers, but that changed. There is a role called a soldier in the infantry detachment. From the lowest level, from the level of soldier and detachment, the work is regulated. I'm not sure whether the translation "detachment" or maybe "squad" would be better to describe what I've just described.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, let's just imagine that you have a unit of military policemen from one brigade, a unit of military policemen from the corps, some battalion soldiers from another brigade, and a unit from a Main Staff regiment, and that they are working on the same task. Would that, under these rules, qualify as a joint task?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In keeping with these rules, this may be considered a joint task. In order to establish who should be in charge and responsibility in terms of the command of all the units which are present in the execution of such a task, it has to be established what the rank and the size of each of the units are, and, also, it should be established by the function and the rank of all the officers who are present there, and based on that, it may be established which of the officers is the most senior one and who should be in command of such a joint task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I suppose, equally, one could have been appointed, couldn't he?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In any case, that would be better. If the superior who sends various units to perform this joint task, and they come from all the different areas, the most appropriate situation would be to appoint an officer in advance who would be in command of all these force. In the war in Bosnia and the Army of Republika Srpska, there were very frequent situations when the so-called temporary compositions were formed of various units from various areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want just to leave, as it were, the rules alone and go back to something we were discussing yesterday. As a matter of practical reality, you knew the sort of soldiers who comprised your battalions. What do you think their reaction would have been to the presence of an officer of the rank of colonel amongst them apparently giving them orders?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At this point, I think the hypothetical needs, if it's reflecting the reality, why don't we just go there because otherwise it's so massively broad. A colonel showing up at the Zvornik Brigade any time between 1992 and 1995 could mean innumerable things, which don't help us, but if we're going to the events we know of, just go there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll particularise. I mean in July 1995. That's enough, isn't it? And you can cross-examine about it later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think if we're dealing with hypotheticals, we need to be specific to what we're talking about. Again, a colonel showing up on July 3rd or July 2nd to help organise a unit to go to Srebrenica is a much different thing than Colonel Beara coming to the Zvornik Brigade under the context that we're all aware.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: If a colonel from the Main Staff had turned up in a village near to Zvornik and had ordered some of your battalion soldiers to guard a school, Mr. Pandurevic, how do you think they'd have reacted to that order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, without doing the guess-work, those people would have carried out the order. You have to be aware of how the military functions. The soldiers of the Zvornik Brigade didn't have the -- didn't frequently have the opportunity to see a colonel in Zvornik, and all those who served in the JNA also knew that they would mostly see junior officers, captains, but they would rarely meet majors and higher-ranking officers. So that rank has a certain authority, but the person who has a higher rank or position doesn't necessarily have more knowledge. But that is, in fact, how things should work.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to leave that topic and these regulations. During the period that you were commander of the Zvornik Brigade, were you required to carry out combat activities in areas outside the brigade's area of defence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the very beginning, in December 1992 when I arrived in Zvornik, this wasn't something I was asked to do. The brigade wasn't even capable of doing that. In January, there was an urgent case to deal with. It had to do with sending in a unit to assist the Bratunac Brigade. They were defending the village of Kravica. But later on in the course of the war, this is something which because frequently done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you the only officer from the Command of the Zvornik Brigade who was sent elsewhere with units by order of the corps or other high command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't the only one. I was sent out, as well, but my Chief of Staff often went too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And was that something that endured throughout the whole of the war?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at various periods of time, and for a certain period of time we'd be outside our zone of defence. That concerned myself and the Chief of Staff. But this isn't good practice, and it's rarely done in organised armies. You don't usually have a commander of the brigade leaving the brigade and going off to carry out another task with other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to have a look, please, at P3379. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And this is -- well, you can tell us. What is this document dated the 27th of September, 1994?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a document I sent to the corps command, to the commander personally, and in this document I requested an amendment to his order, the order according to which Dragan Obrenovic was to be appointed as the commander of a Drina Corps battalion which was to go to the zone of operations of the 2nd Krajina Corps. And as an explanation, I referred to certain situations in which either Obrenovic or myself were absent. I said we were rarely in the command of the brigade together, and that could cause serious problems for us when it came to commanding the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What sort of problems did that cause?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the brigade had very few professional officers and since the commander and Chief of Staff were the men who were most frequently in the field and had a direct influence on the life and work of the brigade, well, if one was absent, and that amounts to 50 per cent of the staff, then we have a serious problem. That's quite evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Perhaps it's worth pushing that. What sort of serious problems arise when one or other of you can't get out to the soldiers in the line?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then the battalion commanders and the company commanders are those who have to do their best to carry out the tasks they received from the Brigade Command, but it was very difficult for them to do this, given their professional qualities. If you wanted to single out 50 soldiers from the brigade, from various battalions, in order to send them outside the brigade's zone, well, then either the commander or the Chief of Staff would personally have to go to the battalion concerned, and with the assistance of the battalion commander they would have to separate or single out such men.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just before we leave this document, I want to look at the -- as it were the -- towards the bottom of it, where it says: "We also proposed detailed analysis of the corps commanding personnel so we can see who were the ones we can count on and get rid of extras." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've already said what you can see here. Perhaps I wouldn't say that now, but at the time, as I was a young man, inexperienced, I said that. I addressed the corps commander in quite strident terms. I was forced to do so because there were officers, there were lieutenant colonels and colonels in the corps command who were never ready to lead a brigade or battalion outside the corps zone, or there were officers from other brigades who rarely left their zones of defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when you were absent from the Brigade Command, who was in command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was absent, my deputy, Dragan Obrenovic, was in command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 7D462, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 11th of April of 1993, the appointment according to standard wartime formation, an order of the Drina Corps. You tell us what this is.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an order on appointing someone to a certain position in the army. The commander of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic, issued this order in which Dragan Obrenovic was appointed as the Chief of Staff and also as the deputy commander of the 1st Zvornik Light Infantry Brigade. It's a textbook example of such an order, and in this order he was assigned permanent duties, a permanent position, and these were duties that he was to perform throughout the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Whose deputy was he upon appointment in April 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I only ask because we looked at a document yesterday that showed that you, in fact, were not formally appointed until October. So according to the documents we've looked at, in April of 1993 the Zvornik Brigade had a deputy commander but no commander formally. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. One could say that he was officially Petkovic's deputy, but it doesn't say that he's being assigned as the deputy, and then the name isn't mentioned. It just says that he is to be the deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, on each of the occasions you were absent - let's keep it simple - after April 1993, was it necessary to write a special order every time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because this order on his appointment, giving the right or, rather, the duty to act in this capacity when I was absent because otherwise the term "deputy" wouldn't have any sense. So when the commander was absent, he would automatically be the deputy commander, and he would assume command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When would such an order be written?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order on being a deputy is drafted on the basis of the law in the army. We saw that the other day. It says that if an officer cannot be -- cannot carry out his duties, someone will stand in for him. It doesn't say why he's prevented from carrying out his duties. It just says that he may be prevented from doing so. So this is done automatically if the establishment doesn't provide for a deputy. If the establishment does provide for a deputy, and that's the case here, then if it's necessary to replace or stand in for the commander for over a month, then one would have to deal with the status of the person who is standing in for the commander, and one would then have to draft an order on standing in for the commander so that this could be part of that person's personal file. This would then make it possible for one to follow his career clearly and see what duties and responsibilities he had to carry out. There would also be certain financial consequences of such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In relation to Dragan Obrenovic, in terms of his authority and responsibility, did it make any difference on occasions when you were absent if a special order for a more-than-month's absence was written or not?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In terms of his responsibilities and duties that arise from the rules on the responsibilities of brigade commander, and we've seen those rules, well, in terms of those responsibilities nothing would be different. He has the same duties and responsibilities as brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, approximately how many times between December 1992 and the end of the war were you absent from the Command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my recollection, it was on about ten occasions, no more.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how many of those occasions exceeded a duration of one month?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the case on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can you tell us when those two occasions occurred?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time was at the beginning of January 1995 up until the 20th of March, 1995, and the second case was in August and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we saw from a document we were just looking at, at the end of December 1994, that you were complaining of health problems. What was the reason for your absence between January and March of 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in January 1995, I was feeling the consequences of my wounding in August 1992, and it was necessary to operate on my spine, and I went to the military hospital for the operation, and after that, I had to recover.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to just briefly run through, as it were, the history of that to see where you were and what was happening to you. Can we start with 7D961, pages 3 and 4 in the English, page 3 in the B/C/S. This refers to your referral to a hospital. Where's Meljine, if I've pronounced it correctly, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Meljine is a military hospital which is in the vicinity of Herceg Novi in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, I don't want to interrupt you unduly, but it's the break time that you had asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I was happy to go on a bit longer because we started quite late today, and I can get through these four or five documents in very little time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It would be logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that appears to suggest -- this document appears to suggest that you were there between the 13th and 16th of March?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether that's the right document that shows what you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, let's come on to 7D962, please, and we want the first page in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would suggest the following: As there are a lot of documents here, perhaps we could go through them during the break and put them in chronological order because it will be difficult to proceed like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I can see you're in control of these proceedings, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We've been over it, you and I, Mr. Haynes. Let's have the break. It's perfectly understandable. Let's do it the way he prefers. Let's have a 25-minute break, starting from now, which the time now is 10.20, 10.21.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you can check with your client whether he has gone through the documents and arranged them in a presentable order.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: They were given to him during the break, and I have a note of the pages that should be called up in e-court so that we have a chronology. Can we start with page 5 of this document, both in the English and the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And does that show your presence in a neurosurgical clinic between the 11th of January and the 6th of February, 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a discharge note showing that between 11 January and 6 February 1995, I was hospitalised. But before that, I underwent a course of physical -- physiotherapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Where did you undergo the physiotherapy, and where is this hospital that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a discharge note from the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks. Now can we go back to page 4 in the record. Where is Igalo?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Igalo is also close to Herceg Novi in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And lastly, forward to page 7 in the documents. I should just say, that document shows you were in Igalo from the 7th of February to the 1st of March, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the Institute for Physiotherapy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we should lastly have page 7 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that covers a period from the 2nd to the 11th of March and relates to some facility in Visegrad. What was that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During that period of time, I continued physiotherapy in the 2nd Banja in Visegrad upon my return from Igalo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when did you, in fact, return to work at the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I returned on the 19th of March, or maybe one day before or one day later; I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And who was in command in your absence?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dragan Obrenovic was in command.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, are you aware whether any order was written to appoint him deputy commander during that period of absence from January to March?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As deputy commander, he assumed duties automatically when I left. No order was issued, which was a case of injustice on his behalf, and that was the same case with me a year later when I was appointed commander of the Zvornik Brigade. This means that he did not receive the salary that he was supposed to receive, and in his personal file it doesn't say, there is no document to that effect, that he was acting or standing in for the commander, and this was an omission on the part of the commander of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look now, please, at 5D 309, a regular combat report from the 15th of March of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Firstly, can we just have a look at the date and confirm that that's a regular combat report of the 15th of March of 1995 and then briefly go to page 2 to confirm the signature on it as that of Dragan Obrenovic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go back to the first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: While we're doing that: Does that confirm for you your recollection that you had not by then returned back working in the Brigade Command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know that Dragan Obrenovic signed regular combat reports. He signed his name as Chief of Staff, and he was supposed to sign as deputy commander, but -- because that's what the order said. In point 2 of this report, we see that the operations officer states the Chief of Staff, who also represents the commander of the brigade, visited the IKM. That's what the duty operations officer put in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in the Serbian original, what's the word used for "represents"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "stand in for."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, it follows from what you said earlier that if there were ten occasions when you were away from the brigade and two which were more than a month, there were about eight occasions when you were away for less than a month; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And, again, I don't want to ask you to perform a memory test, but doing your best, when was the first time you were away from the brigade after you'd assumed command for a short period of time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, it was sometime in the second part of February 1993. I asked from the corps command to grant me a leave lasting seven days. I sent my request to the corps command to that effect, and I also remember some other cases when I was absent for less than a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we've heard a volume of evidence in this case that in May and June of 1993, you took part in two combat operations, both called "Sword" or "Match." How long were away from the brigade on each of those occasions, and what function did you fulfill in those operations?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards the end of May 1993 and the beginning of June, I participated in Sword 1 in the territory of Gornja Podrinje in the triangle, Visegrad, Rogatica, Cajnice. I was the commander of a temporary unit, of an ad hoc unit from the Zvornik Brigade, which also comprised of some other units hailing from that area where the combat operations were taking place, parts of the 2nd Romanija and parts of the Rogatica Brigades. I commanded the forces that were deployed on the left bank of the Drina River. Also, in mid-June of the same year, I participated in Sword 2, which took place from the direction of Cajnice towards Gorazde, and I was the commander of a combat group under the command of Colonel Masal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the duration of those operations in the time you were away from the Brigade Command in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, I was the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, and while I was in command of these units, it was the deputy commander, Dragan Obrenovic, who was in command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I was just trying to establish how long you were away for on each occasion.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, Sword 1 started on the 25th or the 27th of May and lasted up until the 5th or 6th of June. Sword 2 was planned to continue immediately thereafter. However, the units from the Zvornik Brigade were returned to Zvornik, and only a few days later an order arrived for them to return to the area of Cajnice, and there I stayed for some five or six days, as far as I can remember, in the area of Cajnice, participating in the Sword 2 operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to be clear for the record, and not because I have any doubts, we're talking of 1993, aren't we?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And we'll come back to that a little while later. But I want you now to have a look at 7D1011 [Realtime transcript read in error, "7D0111"] relating to another period that you were away for a short period of time, a document dated the 14th of February, 1944 [sic].

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sure none of us want to know what private affairs you needed to leave for, but it's a request to have six days leave beginning the following day. Do you recall sending that request?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall sending in that request. A few months into working without any breaks, both in Visegrad and Rudo and in Zvornik, I requested a leave to visit my daughter in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall what, in fact, the response of the corps command was to that request, and your comment that: "The Chief of Staff or a person assigned by you shall stand in for me during my absence"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The request did not receive a positive answer immediately. It was granted only a few days later. Major Petkovic, who was the brigade commander before me, was in Zvornik, and I knew that General Zivanovic wanted him to assume the duties of the commander again. In order to be granted the leave, I wanted to make sure that it was granted, I put the sentence that I will be replaced by the Chief of Staff or a person assigned by the corps commander, and if I remember it well, the corps commander appointed Major Petkovic to stand in for me during my absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we have a look at 7D1012, please, a collection of combat reports from the period the 17th to the 21st of February of 1994, and if we can have a look at page 2, please, then page 3, then page 4. Just have a quick flip through them. The contents of the document are not important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'd just like your comment, Mr. Pandurevic, on the way Major Petkovic signs himself in these documents.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here on the screen, I have the English version of a report signed by Petkovic, and in the B/C/S I can see an interim report also signed by Petkovic, and he signed himself as commander, not as standing in for somebody but as the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, but for exactitude, could we say "type-signed," because we see that these aren't actually signed, and I don't think anyone's doing that on purpose, but just so it's clear for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. I can't actually recall whether it's all of them. I'll just take a moment to see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, during the period the 17th to the 21st of February, had you been formally relieved of the command of the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not formally. I was still formally the brigade commander. And here you can see the block signature of Major Petkovic, as it were, and this is a standard procedure used for regular combat reports, just as is the case with those which show either Dragan Obrenovic's name or my name.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I've noticed, of course, that Mr. McCloskey's last interruption, in fact, came before you'd answered my question, and I want you to please consider the block signatures we see on all of these reports in the name of Major Petkovic. What's your comment on the fact that they are type-signed as commander by him?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one of the copies of a regular combat report. Regular or interim combat reports are usually drafted by the duty operations officer. The procedure in the Zvornik Brigade was as follows: The operations officer would draft a report in handwriting. Then he would hand it over to the Staff office, and then it would be typed on a computer. The report would then be signed by the authorised person at a given moment, and then the signed report would be sent to the Communications Centre where it would be encrypted and sent by teleprinter to the designated addressee; hence, on the report you can see the name of the signatory and a block signature but not the actual signature in that person's own handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What is the significance of the fact that he has type-signed this document "Commander"?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, he put his signature on the handwritten document, i.e., on the document typed on the typewriter, and thereafter he could not put it on the encrypted version. The person who wrote the document wrote "Commander" by inertia because Major Petkovic had been the commander previously, and this was just an automatic action for people to put the word "Commander," although they should have put "Standing in for the commander." However, I'm sure that that phrase, "standing in for," was something that the officers of the Zvornik Brigade were not that familiar with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But what does it tell us about the way in which all Zvornik Brigade reports are type-signed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understand your question well, there are reports which are typed, but not signed, either in the original version, hence in the version as we see it on the screen. No single report that was encrypted and handed over in that form can bear a signature, especially not at the receiver, because my signature cannot be encrypted and transferred to Vlasenica in that way. The only thing that can be communicated in this way are my name, my rank, my function; not my signature, as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll approach this from a different direction. Can we have a look at 7D944 in English [sic]. These are not translated into English, but the point is the same as in the last document. We only want to look at the signatures or type-signatures. Can we go to page 2, please. This relates to the period we were just talking about, when you were in hospital at the beginning of 1995. We see that Dragan Obrenovic has type-signed this document "Chief of Staff." How should it have been type-signed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been "Deputy Commander, Major Dragan Obrenovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we, just for the sake of argument, go forward, I don't know, five pages. Let's go to page 6 and have a look at the report there, and we only want to see the signature. And, again, how is that signed, and how should it have been signed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's signed in the same way as the previous document. It should have been signed as "Deputy Commander."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how should the reports sent by Major Petkovic have been type-signed?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, since the corps commander designated him to stand in for the commander, that he didn't have a position in the Zvornik Brigade, he had to sign as deputy commander because in establishment terms, he was not the deputy; he was not in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you say "deputy" or something else? "He should have signed as deputy"; is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as standing in for.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thanks. Now, I just want to finish this particular area of your examination by seeing what your reactions to a couple of propositions are. A year ago, you might remember hearing the evidence of Mr. Richard Butler, and I'm going to read this slowly, and I hope it's adequately translated to you, that this is what he said: "The brigade commander is -- by law and regulation, he has the exclusive right of command. Individuals from outside that formation, even if they are higher-ranking individuals, do not have the authority to interfere with that particular commander's right to command his own brigades." Do you agree with his assessment of the situation in the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This position expressed by Mr. Butler is mainly based on Article 115 of the rules on brigades. I can agree with what he said to the extent that the brigade commander, who performs his duties on the basis of the law and orders from his superior commander, well, his duties can't be interfered with by another officer when the commander is, in fact, in command and has control over his brigade. However, there can be a high-ranking officer sent to the Brigade Command with a certain task in order to carry out certain duties that will be carried out bypassing the brigade commander. He can't take over the command of the entire brigade, but he can carry out certain duties; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: He was then asked by Mr. McCloskey: "So what military process or procedure would have to take place before a brigade commander no longer had command responsibility under these regulations?" And he answered: "He'd have to formally be relieved or relinquish command to the superior next in line that's authorised to either relieve him or accept his relief of command." Do you have any comment to make about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A while ago, we spoke about the law on the army and the provisions that had to do with standing in. It says that an officer who can't perform his duties shall be assigned an officer to stand in for him. This individual doesn't have to be formally relieved of his duties because so long as someone is serving in the army, this person has to have certain duties. If I, as the commander of the Zvornik Brigade, was prevented from performing my duties of command of the Zvornik Brigade because I was in command of some other unit outside the brigade's zone, I was in such a case not formally relieved of my duties. However, I was not in command of the Zvornik Brigade at that point in time. My deputy, pursuant to the establishment rules, did that. This means that there can only be one person in command of a given unit at a given point of time, and that is what the term "unity of command" actually means. I cannot be in command of two units at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And just one last point on this. What about the deputy commander when the commander is away? Does the commander have command responsibility for his deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the brigade commander is prevented from performing his duties and his deputy takes over those duties, he performs the duties of brigade commander pursuant to the law and rules on brigades, and on the basis of an order issued by the corps command, he is directly responsible to the corps command and doesn't take any decisions in the spirit of the command. He takes his own decisions on the basis of orders issued by the corps command. In that sense, he is directly subordinated to the corps command and not to the brigade commander who's prevented from performing his duties for certain reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We're finished now with that topic, but I want to move on to another area of, as it were, the question of the organisation of the brigade. What sort of brigade was the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not easy to describe the Zvornik Brigade by using the rules on brigades. Yesterday, we saw a report here from a Main Staff team. They went into the field, and they assessed the level of combat readiness of the Zvornik Brigade. It was said that it would be possible to form a tactical group consisting of three brigades. The Zvornik Brigade was also called the Light Infantry Brigade. That was part of its title, but light infantry brigades can have no more than 2.000 men, whereas the Zvornik Brigade at various points in time had about 6.000 men. In terms of its equipment, in terms of the number of battalions it had, and in terms of certain other elements, it could have been an infantry brigade or even a motorised brigade because given its strength and the equipment it had, this was made possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Haynes, to interrupt you. Can I draw your attention to the previous question and answer. Your question was: "When the commander is away, does the commander have command responsibility for his deputy commander?" And Mr. Pandurevic answered to the effect that: "He," the deputy commander, "is directly subordinate to the corps command and not to the brigade commander who is prevented from performing his duties for certain reasons." Whether that is fully responsive to your question. While the deputy commander is directly subordinated to the corps commander, and it may be a separate matter whether the commander who is away can command -- can exercise his command function over his deputy commander or not. If you could clarify, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you were engaged with Tactical Group 1 in Operation Krivaja 95, who was in command of Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The corps commander, General Zivanovic, was in command of Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Is that clear enough?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Pandurevic, you were not allowed to interfere with the command of General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours. General Zivanovic was the corps commander. He was superior to all the brigade [Realtime transcript read in error, "corps"] commanders in the Drina Corps, so I couldn't influence his decisions. I received his orders, which I carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were just talking about the, as it were, the size and organisation of the Zvornik Brigade. Can we have a quick look, please, at P -- wait a minute. 7D324, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For the record, before he answers -- you put the question at line 17 -- line 18 of the previous page: "... so I couldn't influence his decisions." I clearly recollect the witness saying: I received his orders and I carried them out. And that's for the purpose of correcting the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: This is a Drina Corps command order on appointment, dated the 20th of September, 1995, sent to the 1st Zvornik Infantry Brigade, and it says: "We cannot enter the orders for appointment that you send for battalions in excess of four infantry battalions anywhere in our files. Thus according to the establishment, you should have four infantry battalions, whereas you have seven. Perhaps it's high time you did something to form your brigade according to the existing establishment. The number of men in the present seven infantry battalions, when combined and divided by five, would give battalions numbering 750 men each, which would be acceptable ..." And then it carries on. What was the purpose of this document that you received from the Drina Corps in September 1995?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were documents similar to this one before, throughout the wartime period. We were unable to organise the Zvornik Brigade and structure it so that it corresponded to what it was supposed to be according to the establishment structure. This was literally impossible. I had to have so many battalions, or I would have had to divide the brigade into two parts. Given the mobilisation plan for the Drina Corps -- well, in the mobilisation plan, it stated that there was a 1st Zvornik Brigade and a 2nd Zvornik Brigade. The second one was never established, so there's an individual from the Drina Corps command here who was responsible for organisational and mobilisation matters, and he insisted that I should restructure the Zvornik Brigade so that it corresponded to what it was supposed to be pursuant to the establishment structure. I couldn't do this because this was a circle that couldn't be squared.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want to have a look now at the scheme of the ideally-organised brigade, as proposed by the brigade rules. So can we have P694, scheme 1, which is at B/C/S page 15, in English, page 4. Can I correct that? We've committed that usual sin of having a page of this translated, and it's not translated in P694. So can we have 7D359, please, which is a translated version of it. 539.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we enlarge the Serbian version of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'll give you a hard copy. This is the structure of an infantry brigade according to figure 1 of the brigade rules of the JNA of 1984. Were the units of the Zvornik Brigade organised according to a scheme precisely similar to this?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, one could say that it was similar. But in terms of size and the number of its units, it wasn't identical to this scheme here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were there functional relationships within that scheme between the organs that we see within the figure there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were functional relationships in this scheme, the relationships -- command relationships, on the whole. You can see that all these units in the lower part of the scheme are under the commander. The other units have relationships through the Staff or through the deputy commander, and through the deputy commander they are linked to the commander. This is similar to Article 10 on the responsibilities of the brigade commander, where it says that the commander has direct command or exercises direct command and also indirect command through his assistants or deputies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And how in practical terms did that mean that, for example, the Engineering Unit of the Zvornik Brigade was run?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the Zvornik Brigade didn't have a combat arms at the level of battalions, it didn't have an engineering battalion, it didn't have a mechanised battalion, it didn't have an ABHO battalion, and so on and so forth, then these units that were equivalent to companies were linked to the Staff, to the Chief of Staff, or to some of the deputy [as interpreted] commanders. So with reference to the Engineering Company, the chief of engineering, apart from the duties he had with regard to that company, the duties he had to monitor the company, train them, well, in addition to those duties he was authorised by me to issue direct tasks to those units, to assign direct tasks to those units. I almost never directly assigned a task to the commander of the Engineering Unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you deal with the same question, please, in relation to the Signals Unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Signals Unit, and for a while the Reconnaissance Platoon that we had, were units that were attached to the Staff. The Signals Unit was directly linked to the signalling chief. He was in charge of the unit, and the Chief of Staff was in command of it through him as well. I received information on that unit through the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the Military Police Unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Military Police Company, as you can see in the scheme, was linked to the security organ, but in my order on the reorganisation of the brigade, I said that the Police Company should be attached to the Staff. It was linked to the chief of security, too, and he, together with the Chief of Staff, would usually issue orders to this unit. Both of them reported to me or provided me with information on the situation in this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Since you've referred to it, let's look, please, at 7D806, the reorganisation order of the 21st of March, 1994. And, again, Mr. Pandurevic, because this is a document with a few pages in it, it might be quicker for you to have a hard copy so that we can -- you can read it ahead of us. Is this the reforming order that you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And to summarise it, what was it you sought to achieve by this order in March 1994?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was trying to achieve something similar to what the corps commander warned me about in the order of September 1995. I was told that I should reduce the brigade to the lowest possible number of organisational units because the command brigade, given its size, couldn't serve all the units that were linked to the brigade and given its professional level. So I tried to reduce the number of battalions and the number of direct links to myself because in such a case, the communication channels and command channels are obstructed to a certain extent. So I ordered -- I issued an order to have the brigade reformed in the following way: There was to be a commander with units attached to the Staff. These are units that are directly attached or linked to the Staff or to some of the deputy commanders. You have the Reconnaissance Platoon, the Signals Company, the Military Police Company and the Engineers Company, so these are the units that were not under my direct command. I was in command of them through the intermediary of the Chief of Staff and my assistants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In practical terms, if your Chief of Staff or your chief of security wanted to employee some military policemen, would you necessarily be consulted about that?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since all of these headquarters support units or units attached to the Staff have clearly-defined tasks and duties, and these tasks usually were a repetitive kind, they are carried out to the same extent and same manner every day, so in such a situation it's not necessary to consult me. The individuals who had been authorised by myself had the possibility of directly putting those units to certain use. In the case of the police and in the case of counter-intelligence work and the need in the course of such work to involve the police or to use some kind of equipment, well, in such a case I would not have been informed of the matter. But if it was necessary to use the Police Company to carry out a particular task or if it was necessary to use a platoon from that company, I or someone standing in for me would have been asked to authorise such a task.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: When you mentioned equipment, were you talking about equipment within a military police unit or equipment in some other unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was talking about the equipment of military police. I don't mean major technical means, but mostly the things that the crime prevention police had or what was necessary for counter-intelligence work on the part of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And the Engineering Unit?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Engineering Unit had daily tasks which were always the same, and this was to lay minefields [Realtime transcript read in error, "my fields"], servicing minefields, constructing and maintaining roads, bridges, felling trees, and similar tasks. Every battalion would use the operations duty officer to express the need to engage somebody from the Engineering Unit, and if it was for some ordinary tasks, then the chief of engineers, together with the commander of the Engineering Unit, would go and carry out such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Would that be with or without seeking your authority or notifying you or seeking your approval?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of engineers and the Chief of Staff had my blanket approval to use those units in such a way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, just allied to that, we know the various organs of the brigade had, as it were, corresponding organs within superior command units; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I'd like to go to something that you've already referred to, which is P699, at point 7. That's page 15 in the B/C/S and page 14 in the English. It may be necessary for us to just glance at Article 6, "Functional relationships," as well, but principally I'm going to direct your attention to the second paragraph of Article 7, which says: "Staff relationships between command organs and staff at a higher and lower organisational level are in fact functional relationships governed by the principle of obligatory action in accordance with the requests of the staff organ of the superior command for the purpose of implementing the decision made by the superior commander." In practical terms, how did the organs of the brigade function together with their corresponding organs at a higher organisational level?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about staff relationships, as it were. This is what every modern army is familiar with.
