The first to introduce the staff relationships were the ones that had most success in combat. This means that within a command or a staff, assessments were made, proposals were drafted, and decisions taken. In considering problems and situations, the person who was in charge of decision-taking, which is the commander or the Chief of Staff, were able to take an appropriate decision. Those who made proposals to the person who takes decision have an obligation towards that person. At every level of organisation, at the level of the brigade there is a staff. At the division level, there is also a staff. At the corps level, there is also a staff, and they are identical, basically. They may differ in the number of people that they employ, but in organisational terms they are almost identical. Between these organisational parts of the Staff, the lower -- between the lower command and the organisational parts of the Staff of the higher command, they are the so-called functional relationships which are formed on the basis of the identical scope of work, so that the assistant commander for logistics of a higher command, pursuant to his commander's decision, has the right to communicate with the organ for logistics of the lower command, or some other organ of a higher command, artillery or communications, has a functional relationship with the organ of the corresponding branch of a lower command. However, this functional relationship becomes binding for the staff organs of a lower command, which means that the organ for logistics of a lower command is duty-bound to carry out the requests of the organ for logistics of a higher command with a view to implementing the decisions of the commander of the higher command. So these relationships have not to go through the commander of the lower command or the lower-ranking unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can you give us an example of that relationship in operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This would be the corps command. The corps command has a staff, just like the brigade has a staff, and that staff of the corps command, as the operations command, is almost identical to the brigade staff, especially when we're talking about infantry and motorised brigades. The organs of the Staff or the Command of the Drina Corps could communicate directly and deal with certain tasks with the corresponding organs of the Staff or the Command of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: A concrete example?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps we could use the example of logistics. We did not have reliable and constant sources of supply. We always made do as we could, so the logistics organs of the Zvornik Brigade were often in communication with the logistics organs of the Drina Corps and even of the Main Staff, and they dealt with the issues and problems at hand, and those communications or those lines of communication did not go through me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to just turn very briefly to one particular organ within the brigade, and that's the security organ. We've looked at the scheme. The chief of security of the brigade was your direct subordinate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I want to have a look now, please, at 7D717 again, Article 11. It's page 5 in both documents, and this is the authority of the commander in the brigade regiment again: "The commander heads the work of the command organs and the officers of the subordinate units, guides the training and education of the entire contingent, the execution of daily tasks, and the maintenance of continuous and full combat readiness. "He takes appropriate measures to continuously maintain and strengthen combat readiness and ensures the brigade or regiment is ready to carry out combat tasks." Let's go directly to point 5: "He is in charge of the security service and personnel affairs within the remit granted to him under special regulations." What are the special regulations referred to, and what are -- what was the extent of your remit to be in charge of the security services under this law?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is of significance for an organisation or a system such as the army is that the internal documents which regulate its functioning and work should be harmonised instead of contradicting each other, but this is not always easy to achieve. In the Communist system, this all originated from the unique concept which was All People's Defence and social self-protection, which was led by the League of Communists, so that some service within the system had the so-called privileged position. Here, in bullet point 5 of the rules on the powers of the brigade, it says that a commander is in charge of the security service and personnel affairs within the remit granted to him under special regulations. This implies the regulations which regulate the work of the organs of security on some issues pertaining to the scope of personnel affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. But what were the limits of the extent to which you were in charge of the security organ or security services?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was regulated by the rules of the security service and the instruction on the management of the security services which was issued by the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we might as well -- we'll turn to that in a little while. But those rules, like many we've looked at before, are rules of the JNA. Was the role and function of the security service under the Army of Republika Srpska precisely similar to the role it had under the JNA?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the security service in the Army of Republika Srpska relied mostly on the rules of the security service that were used by the JNA, i.e., the armed forces of the SFRY, they mostly dealt with the same tasks, but they also had some additional aggravating conditions and obligations, and I mean primarily the war situation, the presence of a number of international organisations of a different nature which could always be engaged in some intelligence work. There were also some problems which appeared due to frequent communication via secret channels between various persons on both sides of the front-line, and that's why I'm saying that their scope of work was very complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, we will look at P2741 now, the instruction you've referred to, and let's start with something that's nothing to do with the detail of the document. Did you have something to do personally with the reasons for the issue of this instruction?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not draft it myself, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That wasn't the question. Why was this instruction issued in the first place?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why it was issued, you should ask the author. He knows the best. In my view, it was issued as an additional explanation for the application of the rules of the security service in the Army of Republika Srpska and as a result of the malfunctioning of the organs and their relationship with all the other organs at all levels, as you can see here. As far as I'm aware of the organisational and establishment structure of the Intelligence and Security Sector of the Main Staff, I believe that in the book of establishment, I believe that it's called "The Intelligence and Security Sector," whereas here an instruction is issued for the management and control of the intelligence -- security and intelligence organs, which means that the security organs were given the most prominent place here. And one more thing I would like to say: The sector in the Main Staff, the security and intelligence sector, was very specific with regard to the organisation of the two similar services in the JNA. The security -- the Intelligence Administration in the JNA was within the General Staff, and it was subordinated to the chief of the General Staff, which means that it was a completely separate service, and its rules were issued by the Federal Secretary for National Defence, whereas the security service was part of the Ministry of Defence, and the chief of the Security Administration was the assistant minister of defence, and its rules are the rules for the work of the security services were issued by the Presidency of the SFRY. In the Army of Republika Srpska, these two services were merged into one sector and were subordinated directly to the commander of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could I ask the general to slow down a little bit. The reporter is having a very difficult time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's a very sensible observation. General, you really are speaking far too fast now, and the danger is we're losing a lot in translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we go to the first paragraph of this instruction, and, firstly, can we establish, is this a document that you received in this form, or was it communicated to you, as it were, differently?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to apologise for going too fast. I'll try to abide by your instruction. This instruction on the management and command of the security and intelligence organs was drafted in the Main Staff, and I'm sure that it certainly arrived at the desk in the Drina Corps. I know that I received an instruction with this content. I don't know whether I first received the instruction from the Main Staff or from the Drina Corps. However, the contents of -- were identical, save in a very little segment, so that means that I was familiar with the contents, but I don't know whether this came first from the Main Staff or the Drina Corps. I can't be sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- just to clear that up, let's have a look, please, if we can, at 7D890. This is a document from the Command of the Drina Corps sent on the 26th of November of 1994. If we go to the last page of this document, we can see that it's signed by somebody called Mile Tomic. Who's he?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at the time, Mile Tomic was the chief of security in the Drina Corps, and as far as I can tell by the signature in pencil, this is not "Tomic," but "Petrovic," which means that somebody else signed on his behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we go back now to the first page of this document, we can see in the English version there is a different introduction to the document. In particular, there's a second paragraph which says: "Any explanations needed will be given by the chiefs of the security and intelligence departments of the corps commands, who will also clarify any matters concerning application of the instructions." When you said that there was something slightly different about what you received from the Corps command, is that what you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I had in mind: The organ of security of the Drina Corps provided this remark and said that any explanations needed will be given by the security organ of the Drina Corps as regards the application of this instruction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, whenever it's convenient.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That is perfectly convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So we'll have a 25 -minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. Apologies for the delay, but we had a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: There's really no need to apologise at all. Before we resume the topic we were dealing with before the break, there are a number of transcription or translation errors - I think they're transcription rather than translation - which have been drawn to my attention, and I thought it would be better to deal with them now rather than rushing to deal with them at the end of the day. The first is at page 13, line 17, and it's already had some modification because it's the answer to Judge Kwon's question, and it appears that in the transcription of Mr. Pandurevic's answer, he said that General Zivanovic was superior to all the corps commanders, and the universal view of everybody behind me is that he said he was superior to all the brigade commanders. It's perhaps best that I deal with it by way of a further question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic, when you answered Judge Kwon's question about your ability to interfere with decisions of General Zivanovic, did you say that General Zivanovic was superior to all the corps commanders or something else?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that General Zivanovic was the commander of the Drina Corps and he was superior to the brigade commanders who were within the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Realtime transcript read in error, "MR. THAYER"] Thank you. And the second which was drawn to my attention, I think, by Ms. Fauveau, is at page 16, line 16, and again, I'll see if it can be cleared up with a question rather than just an assertion by me. Yes. It's the phrase "... Chief of Staff, or to some of the deputy commanders ..." and I think the belief is that in answering a question about how the Engineering Unit of the Zvornik Brigade was run, the general said the Chief of Staff and some of the assistant commanders, because of course there was only one deputy commander, but there were several assistant commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you at any stage today, General, refer to a number of deputy commanders within the Zvornik Brigade or, in answering that question, did you refer to the assistant commanders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This question isn't really in the right context, but I didn't talk about deputy commanders. He had assistants and one deputy. The commander had assistants and one deputy.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. And two minor errors. At page 5, there's a reference to an exhibit as P0111 [sic]. It should be P1011 [sic]. And lastly at page 19, line 12, the Engineering Unit, Mr. Pandurevic often had tasks to lay minefields, didn't they, not to lay your fields?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did the Engineering Unit lay minefields?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Minefields, not my own fields. I didn't have any fields.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's move on. Before the break, you were just looking with us at a document which you received from corps command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one further, since we are in the mood of correcting the transcript, Mr. Haynes and Mr. McCloskey. Page 29, line 3, it's not Mr. Thayer but Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not sure who should be flattered.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You were in the process of looking at this again, at an instruction you received from corps command. So that we're clear, is it your recollection that in late 1994 you received two such documents as commander of the Zvornik Brigade or only one of these two?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I already said that I was certain about the contents of the documents. I became familiar with it in November. I remember that there was snow on the ground. As for which document was the first one to arrive in the Zvornik Brigade, I'm not sure, but I'm familiar with both documents. The Drina Corps document isn't from the corps command but from the Department for Intelligence and Security. It's been signed by Colonel Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, I'm not going to take a long period of time on this topic with you, Mr. Pandurevic. If we look at paragraph 1 of the report, it decrees the way in which the security and intelligence organs will spend their time, and the simple question I have for you as to this is: How was it determined, and who by, what particular task fell under which heading?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure that I fully understand the question because the letters are very small in paragraph 1. Perhaps one could zoom in. It will be easier for me then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In fairness, it's probably better to go back to P2741 because it's a much clearer document altogether, and it doesn't involve us going over the page quite so much. So if we can go back to P2741, which apart from the little passage we've looked at is identical. It would make it easier for everybody, I think.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we have a look at item 1 of the instructions, it has to do with the field of work of the security and intelligence organs of the VRS. It's a little confused, or it's quite confused and contradictory. Under one organ, you have two completely different services, the security organ and the intelligence organ, two different organs, and not a single rule for the intelligence organ states how much work relates to a given field. There are two rules that have been confounded in one paragraph. This should have said only instructions for leading the security organs because the instructions mostly concerned the security organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we look at the paragraph numbered 1, please, rather than the first paragraph in the document, which determines that 80 per cent of the total engagement of the field of work of security and intelligence organs should be taken up with intelligence and counter-intelligence tasks. Was that any change to the position as it had been before the issue of the instruction?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, in the early rules two-thirds of the work of the organ of security was counter-intelligence. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but here it explicitly says that it concerned 80 per cent of their total workload, which means that 20 per cent of their work related to security issues, to military police issues, and command staff issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Coming out of the question I started with: Whether on a day-to-day basis those -- any given work was determined to be intelligence and counter-intelligence or some other form of work, was that determined by you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew what the difference was between counter-intelligence and other matters that the security organ dealt with. I wasn't familiar with the working methods in the field of counter-intelligence, I wasn't familiar with the contents of that work, and I didn't know when my assistant for security was involved in counter-intelligence. What I requested from the corps command, but I never succeeded in obtaining this, was to have the corps commander inform me that my assistant for security would be engaged in particular tasks on the basis of the chief of security of the corps, and I wasn't to be interested in the contents of the work. But I didn't manage to obtain this from the corps commander, so I don't know what sort of counter-intelligence work was involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall when you made that request from corps command?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It took up quite a lot of time because as the brigade commander, I was responsible for the overall level of combat readiness, and that means I was responsible for the situation in the field of command and control; I was responsible for the brigade's training, for their morale; I was responsible for security and for logistics. So I had to be quite free to use the relevant mechanisms to carry out this work. However, I couldn't have full insight into security tasks, so the problems that appeared between the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and the assistant for security -- I won't say between myself and Drago Nikolic on purpose because it wasn't a matter of a personal relationship. I would have acted in the same way if anyone else had been in Drago Nikolic's place. However, I understood that I couldn't be persistent in efforts that I was making.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you or, indeed, could you ask him what work he was engaged in on a day-to-day basis?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that Drago Nikolic is a disciplined officer. He conducted himself in a civilised manner and in accordance with the rules. His relationship to the commander was correct. He attended the Command meetings and briefings, and I didn't ask him about the nature of his counter-intelligence tasks. If he told me he was involved in such a task, I had to believe him, take him at his word. That is -- was not something I could check.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll just briefly go through a couple of other aspects of the instruction and how you understood it. I should just clarify this: Did you ever seek from the chiefs of security of the corps any explanation or clarification or interpretation of the provisions of this instruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clarify that, the "chiefs" somehow got pluralised.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It got pluralised because I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever seek clarification of the instruction in line with the copy of it we've seen from the corps?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never asked this gentleman, Colonel Tomic, to clarify the instructions. I think he dwelled very -- or he remained in that position very briefly. I could have only made such a request from the corps commander, and he, through his assistant for security, would be provided with the relevant interpretation. I only had information on when this -- I only had information according to which the person who drafted the instructions had the commander of the Zvornik Brigade and the commander of the Rogatica Brigade from the Drina Corps in mind, as well as commanders who were preventing the security organs from working efficiently, And the situation remained such as it was. I didn't try to penetrate further into the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Just quickly going to paragraph 2, it reads: "The security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander of the unit or institution of which they form part, but with regard to professional activities they are controlled centrally by the security and intelligence organs of the superior command." In practical terms, what did that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the security and intelligence organs, or, rather, that sector in the Main Staff, was completely subordinate to the commander of the Main Staff, and everything had been totally centralised. Both services had been centralised within the framework of one section, and the commander of the Main Staff, through General Tolimir, his assistant, could successfully control the work of these services, these organs, and assigned tasks to them at lower levels in infantry brigades. These functions were distinct. The assistant for intelligence was in the Staff, and he was subordinate to the Chief of Staff, so the first sentence, that the security and intelligence organs are directly commanded by the commander, is true only with regard to the security organs, not with regard to the intelligence organs in the brigade. I have already said that Drago Nikolic, as the assistant for security, was my subordinate. That's correct. But to what extent? If 80 per cent of his work was counter-intelligence work and the commander didn't have to have any knowledge of this work, I accepted that, and I was only -- I only had -- my assistant for security was only under me to a certain extent. I had 20 per cent control over him, and that's how I acted.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. The paragraph that's caused us a degree of debate during the course of this case, the second paragraph, paragraph 2: "Furthermore, all members of these organs and services are authorised by law to act and work on tasks from their field of work analogous to the authority of members of the Republika Srpska Ministry of the Interior State Security Department." What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't very familiar with the field of work of the MUP, of the State Security, but on the basis of my experience from the JNA, I knew that the security organs had such tasks, but not the intelligence organs. The intelligence organs were in the Command or in the Staff, and they can't have any authorisation from -- the authorisation of state security organs or these responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: So far as you were aware, did that involve any additional powers, or was it really merely a confirmation of their powers and authorities that had existed before?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that according to the rules on security organ, it says that they have the responsibilities of the state organs, but what comes under that field, what these responsibilities involved exactly, I couldn't say precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Very well. Can we look at page 4, which will involve us going to -- sorry, paragraph 4, page 2, and it's really just the second half of that paragraph: "All telegrams and mail of the members of the security and intelligence organ shall be delivered exclusively to them personally, and no other organs of the Command, including the commander, have the right to inspect their contents." Had that been the case before?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. I didn't receive such mail. The method was probably the same earlier on too. However, as far as the reports are concerned, given my responsibilities as brigade commander, I requested that in regular combat reports, under the security situation, one should say what the security organ had to do, and in such regular combat reports you can see that these items aren't very extensive. The operations officer would draft these items. So I wanted all command organs to place everything that they had with regard to corps in regular combat reports that I would sign. I would then be responsible for the contents of such reports. I think that this led to a conclusion between the security organ and myself -- this led to a clash between the security organ and myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And can we then go to the third page and have a look at paragraph 7: "The monitoring of the professionalism, legality, and correctness of the work of the security and intelligence organ shall be carried out exclusively by the first superior organs for security and intelligence affairs, except in that part of their engagement relating to command and staff affairs." What would be a command and staff task?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I apologise for the interruption, but the previous answer doesn't make sense in English, so if we're going to correct these things, perhaps we should do it now. Something led to a conclusion between "myself and security"?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said something led to a clash, not a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. That's how it appears in the transcript, anyway, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's a correction without the removal of the previous wrong statement, so let's continue, and thank you, Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What is a command and staff task or a command and staff affair?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as in the case of all organs of the Staff and Command, the assistant for security or, rather, the chief of the security section has to be involved in the work of the Command or Staff when taking decisions, and he, in a professional sense, has to draft an order that will be signed by the commander, and that involves -- that concerns the contents of Staff and Command duties. Military police work and tasks could also come under this title. The classical -- or textbook examples of security tasks also come under this field. But these Command and Staff tasks involve using the security staff, the Security Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the paragraph as a whole, what does it mean, the monitoring of the professionalism, et cetera, shall be carried out exclusively by the first superior organs for security and intelligence affairs?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it means that this concerns the field of work that consists -- that represents 80 per cent of the security organ's work. It has to do with the control of their professionalism, their legality, and with their work. The security organ from the superior command has to assess this work, and as a result, when a professional assessment is made for the security organ, there is a field that concerns whether the assessment is agreed with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's leave that behind us now, and we've really finished with that section of your examination which involved you, your deputy commander, the subordination of your units, their relationship with superior command, and the security organ, and we're going to go back to, as it were, the historical narrative that we'd stopped when we got to the point where you arrived at Zvornik, but we're actually going to go back a little further than that, please, and start by having a look at P29, Directive 4. When was the first time that you ever saw Directive 4?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I saw it was in the Detention Unit, when I received it as part of the DS material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And if we can move on very quickly from there and look at P3029, the Drina Corps order of the 24th of November of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You've already told us that you became the commander of the Zvornik Brigade on the 18th of November [sic] of 1992. This document was delivered personally to the commander of the Zvornik Brigade. Did you receive it?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. In the transcript, it says "November," whereas it should be December that I became the commander of the Zvornik Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You're quite right. I don't know whether I said the wrong thing or whether somebody else made a mistake, but this document, dated the 24th of November, was it delivered to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this document was not delivered to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And when you arrived at the Command of the Zvornik Brigade, did anybody draw it to your attention?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this document was filed at the Zvornik Brigade, but nobody actually drew my attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, I want you to -- I want to take you back in your narrative to your period in Visegrad, which you told us was between June and December of 1992. Can you tell us a little bit about the general situation on the ground in the Drina Valley at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will gladly do that. However, I can't be brief in explaining that, and I apologise in advance. I did have an occasion to gain an insight into the tactical and operative position of the units of the Army of Republika Srpska almost across the entire valley of the Drina, and I was also aware of the position of the Serbian population and the Serbian settlements in the area. When I say "the valley of the Drina River," I mean the area of Upper Drina Valid which includes the municipalities of Cajnice, Gorazde, Rudo, Visegrad, and Rogatica. I also mean the Central Drina Valley, the area from Skelani to Bratunac, as well as the Lower Drina Valley, the area from Zvornik to Bijeljina. The situation in that area, particularly in the upper and central Podrinje, in the first and second half of 1992 was very difficult and not in favour of the Serbian forces. The Serbian population, in the areas of the municipality of Gorazde, had been expelled from the left bank of the Drina River, and partly they managed to keep the settlements on the right bank of the Drina in the direction of Cajnice. Visegrad was completely cut off and completely encircled without any means of communication towards the Romanija Plateau and Sarajevo. In Central Podrinje, the Serbian settlements had mostly been destroyed and reduced to the territory of the town of Bratunac and partly the village of Skelani. Likewise, in the area of Zvornik, the danger came from the Muslim forces deployed across Konjevic Polje, Cerska, and Kamenica. The only communication between the Sarajevo-Romanija Plateau and the Drina River went across Han Pijesak, Vlasenica, and then via Sekovici, which was a detour, and then Crni Vrh and Zvornik. In that area which I have just described, there were approximately 80.000 and 90.000 inhabitants whose position was not enviable. They were either to defend themselves in the area or cross the Drina River and resettle in Serbia. In short, that would be the description of the tactical situation in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And just to try and reflect that position a little bit, we're going to take a look at three or four documents. Can we have 7D968 placed into e-court, please. This is a document from the 23rd of June of 1992, and, again, this is a document of some length, so it might be easier if the accused had a hard copy to flip through. We'll give him a hard copy, yes. 968.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When this is done, now and later, if any one of you would like to have a look at the document that is being given to the witness, please tell me so, tell us so. While we are waiting, Mr. Ostojic, we received the waiver of your client relative to today's sitting, but I don't recall having seen one covering yesterday's absence for the last session or so. So I would like confirmation from you that he actually told you that he was waiving his right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: He did indeed, Mr. President, and we'll look into that and get you one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The document from the 23rd of June of 1992 describes the situation in a number of villages and the activity of the enemy. Is that one that was familiar to you at that time?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document is a detailed description of the situation that I attempted to describe, and it mentions some very concrete settlements and areas, and it points to the necessity of preserving certain towns and settlements inhabited by a majority-Serb population, and also, a reference is made to an easier communication that has to be established between Zvornik and the Sarajevo-Romanija area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And another Main Staff order, 7D965, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Again, not in great detail, just remind yourself of the document. It's a Main Staff order of the 29th of October. Is it a document that you saw contemporaneously, either in -- that is, in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see the document in October 1992. However, I can see that it was drafted four months after the previous document and that it deals with the -- with similar problems which had not been resolved, although the previous document set out some tasks. This document continues to show that the situation is still very hard in the area and that the entire population needs to be mobilised in the areas of Visegrad, Rogatica, Rudo, Cajnice, Foca, and so on and so forth with an intention to defend the entire area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And then are you aware of any attempts to realise any of the objectives under the order?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from June to December, the combat achievements of the Army of Republika Srpska in the area were very modest or even none. The successes were mostly expressed in documents and reports, and they did not reflect the situation as it was on the ground, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Okay. Just one last document, which is a Muslim document, 7D985.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Does this appear to relate to the geographical area and the problems you've been talking about?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an article from the journal of the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was written on the occasion of the jubilee of the brigade in Hajrudin, a message from Tercuk [phoen] and 206th Vitez Brigade of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and it mostly concerns the territory of Zvornik. This text speaks about the successes of the aforementioned units and the losses suffered by the Chetnik forces, both in manpower and equipment. The rough estimate that is mentioned here is 5.000 Chetniks, 50 tanks that were either destroyed or damaged, and so on and so forth. In my view, this is an exaggeration to a certain extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course. But during the period we're talking about, the second half of 1992, did you have opportunity yourself to see the effect of Muslim offensives on the ground in the Drina Valley?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see the effects mostly in the territory of Gorazde, partly in the northern parts of Visegrad Municipality. However, I read military reports, and from the media I was aware of the hardship of the Serbian civilians and soldiers in the territories of the municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you ever see burnt villages?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did see burned villages, quite a lot of them, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In that period, the period we're talking about, do you know how many Serbian villages were burnt to the ground?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see all of those villages, but I know that in the Command of the Drina Corps, General Zivanovic had a map of all the Serbian villages that were either destroyed or burnt in the territories of the municipalities of Bratunac and Srebrenica. That's where his native village was, and he was very familiar with the region, and I suppose that he had his own personal and emotional reasons to deal with the situation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, we have General Zivanovic's map. Its surrogate sheet is 7D940, and for those of us who don't read Cyrillic, that will show us that the title of the map is "Burned Serbian Villages and Churches from May 1992 to January 1993." We could sit here and count them, Mr. Pandurevic, but we already have, and there are 146 villages on that map marked as being destroyed. Does that sound about right to you?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The map behind my back is the map that I saw in the Command of the Drina Corps. I can see some pieces of paper with ordinal numbers, the names of the villages and the times when they were destroyed. The last number is 146. I would say that this is the total number of villages and hamlets that were destroyed in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: You say "that area." It's not the greatest map in the world. What is the area we're talking about there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the area covered by the municipalities of Srebrenica and Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, we're going to come on, probably tomorrow morning, to some of the combat activities you took part in in 1993. You've told us you didn't know about Directive 4 until you got here to The Hague. When you took part in those combat activities in early 1993, were you aware of any strategic plan that you were taking part in?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I first came to Zvornik and took over the command of the Zvornik Brigade, the only picture that I had before me was the very difficult tactical position and lack of organisation in the Zvornik Brigade, and my main task was to improve its organisation and to make the brigade as efficient as possible and include it in combat. I did not have before me the order of the Drina Corps or Directive number 4. However, as a soldier, I was aware that even without an order or without a command, life itself imposed tasks on me and ordered me to do something. In that sense, at the beginning of January, I launched certain combat activities - very limited, however - just to show some activity, just to show everybody that the Zvornik Brigade was still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: What was the necessity of those activities you began with the Zvornik Brigade?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the map that you showed me yesterday, and we couldn't use it, you could see the position of the Zvornik brigade as it was at the time. We had a battalion in Drinjaca, south of Zvornik, 12 kilometres south of Zvornik. It was completely encircled at the time. We also had Muslim forces at -- within the shooting range from the city. Children and women from Zvornik had already moved out to Serbia. The combat readiness of the brigade was very low. The territory of Crni Vrh was not taken, and there was a constant communication line between the BiH Army forces in Zenica and Srebrenica, and the road leading from Zvornik towards Crni Vrh and Sekovici was very often blocked, and traffic was interrupted by the activities of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In January of 1993, did you first take part in combat activities pursuant to a Drina Corps order; namely, Operation Proboj?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This name, Operation Proboj, would have to mean a lot symbolically. It would be the whole corps or at least two or three brigades that would have to be engaged in that operation. It would last over four to six days, in two stages. However, what we did at that time, under the name of Proboj or "Breakthrough," which was painstaking maneuvering of forces left and right with minimum movements in depth, and the first actions in January were actions at the entrance to Kravica when we tried to stop the breakthrough of the Muslim forces to the Drina River, and after that actions started in the general area of Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: At the tactical level, what did it seem to you was the purpose of the action, the operation?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The main task was to repel the Muslim forces from the town of Zvornik, to prevent the forces to communicate between the 2nd Corps and the 28th Division, which was then 8th Operations Group, and later on, if possible, the aim was to push all those forces even further away from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And what was the apparent intention of your enemy?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The intention of the enemy was to link up the forces of the 2nd Corps on the north and north-west sides of Zvornik with the forces in Kamenica, Cerska, and Konjevic Polje. In the second stage, they would have taken the area on the banks of the Drina River and would -- they would have eliminated any form of the Serbian life in the eastern part of that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Your orders under Operation Proboj, did they seem to you to be justifiable military orders?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those orders, from the military point of view, were absolutely justified and logical. I issued those orders and I received those orders both orally and in a written form, and from time to time I even had a personal communication with the corps commander and the Chief of Staff with this regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: We'll move on to Kamenica. We've had a look at this document before. It's 7D1006, the regular combat report for the 1st of February, 1993. Thank you, it's on the screen. Just remind yourself of what this report says. At the time you wrote the report on the 1st of February, 1993, what was the military situation, what were you engaged in, and what point had you reached?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, during this period the tactical situation of the Zvornik Brigade was much more favourable than it was in December 1992. We had managed to take the area of Kamenica, and on the 1st of February or somewhat later we took Glodjansko Brdo. In November, our forces had been defeated there and we had suffered great losses there. We were also planning on continuing combat operations in the direction of Konjevic Polje. Judging from this report, as we look at it, I -- you can see that I sent an imprisoned enemy soldier to the Muslim forces -- Muslim villages where we expected conflict and offered protection to the civilian population, which was in compliance with the application of the International Laws of War, which was in force in the armed forces of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Let's address that head-on. During the Bosnian conflict, what generally caused population movement, Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The armies which were engaged in the civil war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the one side, the Army of Republika Srpska, and the other side, the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in some parts also the Croatian Defence Council; basically, we are talking about armed populations, civilians that called themselves armies. This was a conflict between people who had lived together and knew each other very well there because they had been neighbours, and in that conflict, if the one side prevailed over the other side, their respective villages and territories would become completely deserted, and they would be taken by the prevailing force. At that time, we could not speak of any trust. Nobody waited for the enemy side to come to the village. Even to this day, we have Annex 7 of the Dayton Accord which has never been fully implemented, and it talks about the return of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Just one more question, and answer it as quickly as you can. Why did you take this step of opening a corridor and apparently ceasing fire in the circumstances you'd reached by the 1st of February, 1993?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The provisions of the International Rules of War say that the commanders of the warring parties in a certain area may establish the so-called safety areas where civilians could be sheltered because civilians could not be objects of military actions. At that time, I could not get in touch with the Muslim commander in order to agree on that. However, I did have a choice to send my prisoner of war there. On the other hand, the International Law of War and the regulations that I was aware of say that the commander can ban the civilians from leaving the encircled area. I did not opt for that. I justified a fire opened on enemy lines by what we call the military necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I think we'll leave that there. I would just like to check that answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you say you justified fire on the enemy lines there?

utterances.speaker: VINKO PANDUREVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any action was justified by military necessity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, we'll leave it there for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Thank you, Mr. Pandurevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Nobody is very happy with that. Is that translation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll clarify it tomorrow because there is another sitting -- another court sitting this afternoon. We'll resume tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.
